title: A full game with a partner
objectives: Run a full market-making game and review every trade.

screens.title: Before the game
screens.prose: In the game ahead you quote width 4 around fair, less 0.5 for each lot you hold. Round the centre to the nearest 0.5. Fair starts at 21. On turn 1 the interviewer buys 1 from you at 23.
screens.question: What is your bid on turn 2?

widget.accept: 19.5: short 1 moves the centre to 21 + 0.5 = 21.5, and the bid is 2 below.

The centre is $21 - 0.5 \times (-1) = 21.5$.

byKey.down: You moved down. Short 1 wants to buy back, so the quote moves up.

screens.title: The full game
screens.prose: Eight turns on the sum of three cards. The interviewer is the counterparty: the results table lists them as `scripted`. They trade four times, each with a price limit. Cards turn before turns 3 and 6. Size 1 or 2, width 1 to 4, limit 3.
screens.question: Finish with a P&L of at least £10 and no rule breaks.

schedule.text: Three cards are dealt face down from a full deck, ace 1 to king 13. Fair is $3 \times 7 = 21$. Width 4 at most, limit 3 either way.
Card 1 is turned: a 4. Fair is now $4 + 2 \times 360/51 = 18.12$.
Card 2 is turned: a 6. Fair is now $10 + 354/50 = 17.08$.

hints.text: After each card, move your centre to the new fair value.
Skew 0.5 for each lot you hold, and keep the width at 4.
Quote 19 at 23, 19.5 at 23.5, then 16.5 at 20.5 twice. Then 17 at 21, 16 at 20, and 15.5 at 19.5 twice, all for 1.

feedback.correct: A full game, updated on every card and every trade.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Update on every card, skew on every trade, and keep the size at 1.

byKey.low: Your P&L is under £10. A stale quote buys from an interviewer who has just seen low cards.
byKey.crossed: Your bid met or passed your ask, so nobody traded. Keep the bid below the ask.
byKey.limit: A quote was larger than your room on one side. Once you are short or long 2, a size of 2 breaks the limit of 3.
byKey.spread: Your width left 1 to 4. Keep the ask at most 4 above the bid.

explain.text: The model sold 1 at 23, and its 16.5 bid missed the interviewer’s sale at 19 after the 4. Then it sold 1 at 20.5 and bought 1 at 16. Short 1 with cash +£27.50, it settled at 15, the last card a 5: +£12.50.

screens.title: Fair after the 4
screens.prose: Now rebuild the fair values you traded on. Before turn 3, the first card showed a 4. The deck held 364 points in 52 cards.
screens.question: What was the fair value of the sum after the 4? Give it to 4 places.

hints.text: The 4 is gone from the deck. What do the other 51 cards average?
They hold $364 - 4 = 360$ points: $360/51$ each.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Two unseen cards each average $360/51$.

byKey.seven: You used 7 for each unseen card. The 4 left the deck, so they average $360/51$.
byKey.whole: You divided by 52. Only 51 cards are left.

explain.text: The 51 cards left hold 360 points, $360/51 = 7.06$ each. Two of them plus the 4 give $308/17 = 18.12$. Low cards out of the deck push the average of the rest up.

screens.title: Fair after the 6
screens.prose: Before turn 6, the second card showed a 6. Two cards are known, one is unseen.
screens.question: What was the fair value of the sum after the 6?

hints.text: Now 50 cards are left. What do they hold?
$364 - 4 - 6 = 354$ points in 50 cards.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the known 10 to one card from the 50 left.

byKey.seven: You used 7 for the last card. The 50 left average $354/50 = 7.08$.
byKey.old: That is the fair value before the 6.

explain.text: The known cards sum to 10. The last card averages $354/50 = 7.08$, so fair is $427/25 = 17.08$. The true third card was a 5, settling at 15.

screens.title: Had it been a king
screens.prose: Keep the model run's trades: short 1 with cash +£27.50. Suppose the third card had been a king, 13, not the 5.
screens.question: What would the model run's P&L have been, in pounds?

hints.text: What is the true sum with a king?
Short 1 against a cash of 27.50: $27.50 - 23 = 4.50$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract the new sum, 23, from the cash.

byKey.old: You kept the true sum at 15.
byKey.sign: You subtracted the wrong way. Cash 27.50 less 23 is positive.
byKey.long: You added the sum. Short 1 owes it.

explain.text: With a king the sum is 23 and the P&L is $27.50 - 23 = 4.50$. That is 8 less, one point for each point the card rose from 5. The same quotes earn £12.50 or £4.50, so the P&L alone does not grade them.

screens.title: A game with no trades
screens.prose: In another round the interviewer never trades. Eight turns pass. Your P&L is £0.
screens.question: How do you review this game?

options.text: Check each quote: centred on the fair value of its moment, the width right, the moves after each card
There is nothing to review: no trades, no P&L
options.why: You reviewed only the P&L. The quotes are the work, and they can still be wrong.

options.text: Quote tighter next time, to get trades
options.why: You assumed no trades means too wide. The interviewer may have chosen not to trade at any price.

options.text: It was a bad game, because it made no money
options.why: You judged by the outcome. With no trades your edge is zero whatever your quotes.

hints.text: What did you produce in each turn, trade or not?
Every turn you gave a quote.
Review each quote against the fair value of its turn.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. A game with no trades still has eight quotes to grade.

byKey.nothing: You reviewed only the P&L. The quotes are the work, and they can still be wrong.
byKey.tight: You assumed no trades means too wide. The interviewer may have chosen not to trade at any price.

explain.text: With no trades the edge is zero, so the P&L says nothing. The review is about the quotes: centre, width and each move. That is what the interviewer marked all along.

screens.title: P&L trade by trade
screens.prose:
Each trade's P&L is its edge against the true value $V$. A sale of $n$ at price $p$ earns $n(p - V)$; a buy earns $n(V - p)$. The game's P&L is the sum:
$$\text{P\&L} = \sum_{\text{sales}} n(p - V) + \sum_{\text{buys}} n(V - p).$$
screens.question: The stale run sold 1 at 23 and bought 1 at 19 twice, with $V = 15$. What is its P&L, in pounds?

hints.text: Work out each trade's edge.
The sale earns $23 - 15 = 8$; each buy earns $15 - 19 = -4$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the three edges: $+8$, $-4$ and $-4$.

byKey.sale: You counted only the sale. The two buys at 19 each lost 4.
byKey.sign: You counted the buys as gains. Buying at 19 something worth 15 loses.

explain.text: The sale made 8 and the two buys lost 4 each. Both buys came after low cards, from someone who knew: adverse selection. Splitting the P&L by trade shows where it came from.

screens.prose: Code the post-game review: the P&L of each trade at the true value, and the total. The tests use the model and stale blotters.
screens.question: Complete `review_game`.

widget.how: Check runs 6 hidden tests. The result is a tuple: the list of per-trade P&Ls, then the total.

A buy earns `size * (true_value - price)`.
Collect the per-trade values in a list, then return it with `sum(per)`.

explain.text: The model's trades give 8, 5.5 and −1, a total of 12.5. With a king the same trades give 0, −2.5 and 7: 4.5. The per-trade view shows which quotes did the work.

screens.title: The desk's daily review
screens.prose: A trading desk reviews every trade each evening. Today: sold 100 shares at £50.20, bought 60 at £49.90, bought 40 at £50.30. The close, the value used, is £50.00.
screens.question: What is the day's P&L, in pounds?

hints.text: Find each trade's edge against £50.00.
The sale earns $100 \times 0.20 = 20$; the first buy $60 \times 0.10 = 6$.
The last buy loses $40 \times 0.30 = 12$: $20 + 6 - 12 = 14$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the three edges against £50.00.

byKey.nolast: You left out the last buy. Paying 50.30 for shares worth 50 lost £12.
byKey.sign: You counted the last buy as a gain. It was paid above the close.

explain.text: The sale made £20 and the first buy £6. The last buy, at 50.30, lost £12: it bought back the short after the price had risen. The desk asks why that trade happened, as you did for turn 6.

screens.title: With a real partner
screens.prose: The app played the interviewer for you. A real partner is better: they can trade on a whim, interrupt, and hear you. Practise aloud with a partner, as interview guides advise.
screens.question: How should your partner run a practice round?

options.text: Pick cards and trades in secret, keep a watch, and hear your update after each trade
Trade only at prices that make you money, to build confidence
options.why: You asked for an easy partner. A real interviewer trades when you are wrong.

options.text: Let you play silently, then check the final P&L
options.why: You skipped the speaking. The partner is there to hear the reasoning.

options.text: Use the same cards every time, so you can learn them
options.why: You memorised the game. A fresh deal each round tests the updating.

hints.text: What can a partner do that the app cannot?
They can hear you and trade when you slip.
A secret script, a watch and an update after each trade.

feedback.correct: A secret script, a watch, and your update after each trade.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The partner's job is to test and to listen.

byKey.easy: You asked for an easy partner. A real interviewer trades when you are wrong.
byKey.silent: You skipped the speaking. The partner is there to hear the reasoning.

explain.text: A partner who trades unpredictably tests your updating. A watch keeps the pace of a real round. Hearing each update is the point, since interviewers mark it.

ideas: A full game updates the fair value on every card and skews the quote on every trade.
Review a game trade by trade: edge, adverse selection avoided, inventory reduced.
Judge the quotes, not the final P&L: the same quotes made £12.50 with a 5 and £4.50 with a king.

quiz.prose: Short 2 with fair 17.08, you skew 0.5 a lot and quote 16 at 20. The interviewer sells you 1 at 16.

For edge: 16 is below fair

options.text: Because the interviewer knew the cards
options.why: A seller who knows would make this trade lose, which it did against 15. The model bought to cut risk.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at why the bid sat at 16.

explain.text: The bid was 16 because the centre moved up 1 for the short 2. That made the bid more likely to trade, buying back risk. Against the true 15 it lost £1, a fair price for halving the position.
